Situation1: Their partner had a mildly stressful day at work and mentions it casually.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: I sat at the kitchen table, my laptop open, notes scattered everywhere. My husband walked in, dropped his bag, and sighed. “Work was a bit much today,” he said, rubbing his temples. I looked up, catching the tiredness in his eyes. I knew he wanted me to listen, to offer comfort, maybe just sit with him and let him vent. But my phone buzzed—an urgent message from a colleague about the policy proposal I’d been working on for weeks. The city council was meeting tomorrow, and I needed to finalize my argument against a rule that would make it harder for refugee applicants to access services. People were counting on me to speak up, to be their voice. My husband’s voice, soft and expectant, pulled me one way; the call to action, loud and insistent, tugged me the other. My heart ached with the weight of both worlds, knowing I couldn’t give my all to both at the same time.
